en: Taal Volcano erupts when hot magma rises through a vent beneath Lake Taal, releasing immense underground pressure.
The Cagayan River carries eroded soil from the Sierra Madre mountains, depositing it to form a wide delta.
The Amihan brings cold, dry air from Asia to the Philippines, causing the cool, dry season from November to February.
Tubbataha Reefs thrive because warm, shallow, sunlit waters allow photosynthetic corals to build massive calcium carbonate structures.
Tiwi Geothermal Power Plant generates electricity by using natural underground steam from magma to spin large turbines.
The Banaue Rice Terraces prevent soil erosion by carving flat, stone-walled steps that slow down fast-flowing rainwater runoff.
Puerto Princesa Subterranean River formed when slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the porous limestone bedrock over millions of years.
Typhoons gain strength over the warm Pacific Ocean because evaporated seawater releases heat, fueling the storm's powerful rotating winds.
The tamaraw survives only on Mindoro because deep ocean waters isolated the island, preventing the species from migrating to other landmasses.
The Philippine Trench generates frequent earthquakes because tectonic plates constantly push and scrape against each other deep underground.
Lake Lanao remains a freshwater lake because continuous rainfall replenishes it, while the Agus River constantly drains excess water.
The Sierra Madre mountains cause heavy rain on their eastern side because their high peaks force moist storm winds upward.
